Unit 6A · Speaking & Grammar

Will we be happier
in the future?

An unhurried lesson in the art of prediction — with will and won't. Listen to real voices, learn the grammar, and picture the years ahead.

Ninety minutes — entirely in English
Teacher~90 min. Guided, one section at a time — use the rail above or Back / Next. Both listenings have the real audio built in (play, seek, slow to 0.75×, back 10s). Answer keys and audioscripts sit behind buttons. Toggle these notes with the Teacher button — the student won't see them unless you switch them on.
Warm-up

Before we begin

Just conversation — no right answers yet. Picture the world twenty years from now.

What is one thing that will change a great deal?
Are you an optimist or a pessimist about it all?

We'll return to these at the very end. Which one matters most to you?

Listening · 6.1

Five voices, one question

Five people answer: “Will we be happier in the future?” Let's listen.

Speaker 1

Audioscript · 6.1

Speaker 1 These days, in general, people are much healthier. We know a lot more about the importance of eating well and we try to keep fit, and this makes us happier. In the future, I think we'll be more careful about what we eat. I already go running three times a week — the next thing I should do is eat less chocolate!

Speaker 2 Oh, less happy, definitely. People are waiting longer to have children and start a family, usually because their careers come first. I think this will continue in the future and for many people it'll be too late. And I think a happy family life is really important, especially later in life.

Speaker 3 For me, the most important thing to be happy is to have a good career, a job which you really enjoy doing. But I think in the future this won't be easy, because our jobs will be more difficult. People will work harder and I don't think we'll have as much free time, so in general we'll be much less happy than we are now.

Speaker 4 Will we be happier? Definitely. It'll be easier to earn lots of money and that's what's important. More people will be able to buy big houses, go on lots of holidays and buy all the nice things that they want.

Speaker 5 Yes, I think so. Look at social media, for example. It's simple to meet people now and it'll be even easier in the future. Having a busy social life makes you happy, and it won't be hard to make friends in the future.

4c

Your view

Speaking. Which predictions do you agree or disagree with — and why?

Speak in full: “I agree with number three because…” A note, if you wish:

TeacherPlay the whole track once for 4a (gist) — reassure her she needn't catch every word. Play again for 4b; pause after each relevant speaker if useful. Answers 4a: 1 yes · 2 no · 3 no · 4 yes · 5 yes. The audioscript button gives a third listen or a read-along. For 4c, push for because + a reason.
Grammar

will for predictions

The grammar beneath everything those five people said. Read it, then match each rule to their words.

Grammar — 15 min
The rule
a
Use will + infinitive to make predictions about the future.It'll be more difficult to find a good job.
b
Use won't + infinitive for negative sentences.In the future, we won't have so many problems.
c
We often use I think + will in spoken English.I think we'll be healthier.
d
The negative form is I don't think + will.I don't think we'll work as much.
Positive
I / we / they will ('ll) + verb
Negative
I / we / they won't + verb
Good to knowI (don't) think + will is far more common than will / won't alone in everyday speech — so it's well worth practising.
5

Match the rules

Match each rule a–d with the prediction from the listening.

i“It won't be hard to make friends.”
Rule b — won't
ii“It'll be easier to earn lots of money.”
Rule a — will
iii“I don't think we'll have as much free time.”
Rule d — I don't think
iv“I think we'll be more careful about what we eat.”
Rule c — I think
TeacherConcept-check before matching: “Do we use will for the past, present or future?” (future) — “For predictions or fixed plans?” (predictions). Answers: 1‑b · 2‑a · 3‑d · 4‑c. Drill the contractions (we'll, it'll, won't) chorally — they're the focus of the next listening.
Listening · 6.2

Catch the contraction

Native speakers slip will into 'll. Let's train your ear to hear the difference.

Listening — 10 min
6a

Which do you hear?

Listen and choose the form you actually hear.

iI don't think be less happy.
iiPeople go out much.
iiiI think have more time for our friends.
iv be easier to meet new people.
vI don't think sleep as much.

Audioscript · 6.2

i  I don't think people will be less happy.

ii  People won't go out much.

iii  I think we'll have more time for our friends.

iv  It will be easier to meet new people.

v  I don't think we'll sleep as much.

6b

Listen & repeat

Say them aloud. Copy the rhythm — let 'll stay quick and light.

Replay the audio and echo each sentence after the speaker. Little and light beats loud and slow.

Ear tipwe'll sounds like “wheel”, it'll like “it-ul”, and won't rhymes with “don't”.
TeacherThe teaching point is contractions. Play once for 6a, elicit that the difference is the contracted form. For 6b, drill chorally then individually — model the reduced 'll yourself. Answers: 1 people will · 2 won't · 3 we'll · 4 It will · 5 we'll.
Grammar in practice

Compose a prediction

Turn each set of prompts into a full prediction. Say it first, then write it — reveal the model to compare.

Writing — 12 min
6c

Make predictions

Use will / won't — and I think / I don't think. Add small words like a, the, more, as where needed.

TeacherItem 1 is the worked example. Accept natural variation — I don't think we'll… and I think we won't… are both fine, as are much / as much. The checker is lenient (it ignores contractions and punctuation); use “Reveal” to compare and elicit self-correction rather than simply marking right or wrong.
